question: Which original studies (RCTs and NRSIs) compare larger versus smaller RBC volume per transfusion for anemia in hospitalized adults, children and preterm neonates?

S1.title: Transfusion volume in infants with very low birth weight: a randomized trial of 10 versus 20 ml/kg

S2.title: Wong 2005, high volume versus standard volume PRBC transfusion in premature infants

S3.title: Choi 2021, 20 versus 15 mL/kg transfusion in preterm infants

S4.title: Mallett 2016, 20 versus 15 mL/kg crossover in VLBW infants

S5.title: Chen 2023, 20 versus 15 ml/kg in preterm infants

S6.title: von Lindern 2011, cohort of two NICUs 15 versus 20 ml/kg

S8.title: Chantepie 2023, single versus double RBC per transfusion

S9.title: Byun 2023, pilot factorial trial in AML

S10.title: Bowman 2019, single-unit policy in malignant haematology

S11.title: Marco-Ayala 2024, single-unit policy in autologous HSCT

S12.title: Heyes 2017, single-unit policy on medical wards

S13.title: Significant reduction of red blood cell transfusion requirements by changing from a double-unit to a single-unit transfusion policy in patients receiving intensive chemotherapy or stem cell transplant

S14.title: Ma 2005, single-unit transfusion and allogeneic exposure

S15.title: Bosch 2021, Hb-triggered single-unit policy for haemato-oncological inpatients

S16.title: Comparison of Hematocrit Change in Preterm Neonates with Birth Weight Based Versus Formula Based Packed Red Blood Cell Transfusion

S17.title: A comparative cohort study on transfusion practice and outcome in two Dutch tertiary neonatal centres

claims.text: Infants with birth weight 500 to 1,500 g were randomly assigned to 10 or 20 mL/kg red blood cells; post-transfusion hemoglobin was 14.2 versus 12.0 g/dL with 20 versus 10 mL/kg.
Mallett: 22 hemodynamically stable VLBW infants in a randomized crossover study of 20 versus 15 mL/kg; hemoglobin 13.2 versus 11.8 g/dL.
Chen: 73 newborns received 20 ml/kg and 78 received 15 ml/kg; transfusions 1.9 versus 2.6.
TRACT: 3196 African children with hemoglobin below 6 g/dL randomised to 20 versus 30 mL/kg; 28-day mortality 3.4% versus 4.5% (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.08).

Byun: pilot randomised factorial trial in 91 AML patients on chemotherapy comparing Hb trigger 7 versus 8 g/dL and single versus double unit per transfusion; units per transfusion did not change total RBC use, outcomes or bleeding.

Marco-Ayala: 187 patients under a single-unit policy versus 153 historical double-unit patients in autologous stem cell transplant; RBC use fell 32%; length of stay, discharge Hb and 30-day mortality did not differ.
Chantepie: patients with acute leukaemia or transplant randomly assigned to single RBC or double RBC per transfusion.
Wong: randomised trial of high volume (20 ml/kg) versus standard volume (15 ml/kg) PRBC in premature infants.
Choi: 39 infants born before 34 weeks randomly allocated to 20 versus 15 mL/kg.
von Lindern: cohort comparison of 15 ml/kg in Unit A and 20 ml/kg in Unit B in extremely premature infants.
Bowman: before-after comparison in malignant haematology of a single-unit RBC transfusion policy.
Heyes: six months before and after implementation of a single unit policy on eight general medical wards; single-unit orders rose from 30% to 53%.

conclusion: Seventeen studies compare larger with smaller RBC volume per transfusion; neonatal trials show higher haemoglobin with 20 versus 10 or 15 mL/kg, TRACT is the only paediatric volume trial, and adult evidence is single versus double unit mostly in haematology.
